questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish integration governance from the integration-design patterns covered in Chapter 2?
options: Governance is a purely legal requirement with no architectural relevance
Governance is the ongoing organizational discipline keeping the entire landscape of integrations healthy over time, as distinct from designing any single integration well
Governance only applies to integrations built using MuleSoft
Governance and pattern design are the same activity under two different names
questions.explain: Chapter 2's patterns are about designing one integration well; governance is the organizational discipline that keeps the whole landscape of many integrations healthy as it grows, as people change, and as connected systems evolve.

questions.q: What specific problem does an integration inventory exist to prevent?
options: It prevents any integration from ever failing
A routine change to a field or API version silently breaking an integration nobody remembers exists, because it was never written down anywhere searchable
It prevents the need for any error-handling standard
It replaces the need for a named owner on each integration
questions.explain: Without a maintained inventory, an organization doesn't actually know what integrations it has, so a routine change can silently break something nobody remembers exists — exactly the gap an inventory closes.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say ownership should be assigned to a role or team rather than relying on the original developer?
options: Because the original developer is always the best choice and this is purely a formality
Because people leave, and an integration with no durable ownership becomes an orphaned asset that keeps running until it fails with nobody positioned to fix it quickly
Because Salesforce requires all integrations to be owned by an admin specifically
Because ownership has no bearing on how quickly an issue gets resolved
questions.explain: Tying ownership to the original developer fails as soon as that person leaves. A role or team-based ownership model keeps accountability durable even as individual people move on.

questions.q: What is the purpose of integration standards, per this lesson?
options: To guarantee zero downtime across every integration
To give every team shared conventions — naming, error handling, credential storage, documentation — so the fiftieth integration doesn't require relearning decisions the first ten already settled
To eliminate the need for a review process entirely
To require every integration to use exactly the same middleware product
questions.explain: Standards exist so an organization doesn't relitigate the same design decisions (naming, retry approach, credential handling, documentation format) on every new integration, building consistency across a growing landscape.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe "nobody knows what this integration does anymore" as a governance failure rather than a technical one?
options: Because the integration itself may still be running correctly; the organization lost the institutional knowledge to safely change, retire, or understand it, due to missing inventory, ownership, and documentation
Because it means the integration's code must contain a bug
Because it only happens when an integration uses the Bulk API
Because it is always caused by a network outage
questions.explain: The integration may be functioning perfectly; the failure is organizational — no inventory, ownership, or documentation standard ever captured the institutional knowledge needed to safely understand, change, or retire it.
